title: The sons of the gods and the work of Jesus
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτά φησιν ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος ὡς φιλομαθής τις Ἕλλην καὶ τὰ Ἑλλήνων πεπαιδευμένος ὅτι οἱ μὲν παλαιοὶ μῦθοι Περσεῖ καὶ Ἀμφίονι καὶ Αἰακῷ καὶ Μίνωϊ θείαν σπορὰν νείμαντες (οὐδ᾿ αὐτοῖς ἐπιστεύσαμεν) ὅμως ἐπέδειξαν αὐτῶν ἔργα μεγάλα καὶ θαυμαστὰ ἀληθῶς τε ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον, ἵνα μὴ ἀπίθανοι δοκῶσι· σὺ δὲ δὴ. τί καλὸν ἢ θαυμάσιον ἔργῳ ἢ λόγῳ πεποίηκας; ἡμῖν οὐδὲν ἐπεδείξω, καίτοι προκαλουμένων ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ σε παρασχέσθαι τι ἐναργὲς γνώρισμα, ὡς εἴης ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ παῖς. πρὸς τοῦτο δὲ λεκτέον ὅτι δεικνύτωσαν ἡμῖν Ἕλληνες τῶν κατειλεγμένων τινὸς βιωφελὲς λαμπρὸν καὶ παρατεῖναν ἐπὶ τὰς ὕστερον γενεὰς καὶ τηλικοῦτον ἔργον, ὡς ἐμποιεῖν πιθανότητα τῷ περὶ αὐτῶν μύθῳ, λέγοντι ἀπὸ θείας αὐτοὺς γεγονέναι σπορᾶς. ἀλλὰ γὰρ οὐδὲν δείξουσιν οὐδὲ μικρῷ ἐλάττω περὶ οὓς ἀνέγραψεν ἄνδρας ὧν παρέστησεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς. ἐὰν ἄρα μὴ ἐπὶ μύθους ἀνάγωσιν ἡμᾶς Ἕλληνες καὶ τὰς παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς ἱστορίας, θέλοντες ἡμᾶς μὲν ἐκείνοις ἀλόγως πιστεύειν τούτοις δὲ καὶ μετὰ πολλὴν ἐνάργειαν ἀπιστεῖν· αὐτοί φαμεν οὖν ὅτι τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τὸ ἔργον ἡ πᾶσα ἔχει ἀνθρώπων οἰκουμένη, ᾗ παροικοῦσιν αἱ τοῦ θεοῦ διὰ Ἰησοῦ ἐκκλησίαι τῶν μεταβαλόντων ἀπὸ μυρίων ὅσων κακῶν. καὶ ἔτι γε τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐκστάσεις μὲν διανοίας ἀνθρώπων ἀφίστησι καὶ δαίμονας ἤδη δὲ καὶ νόσους, ἐμποιεῖ δὲ θαυμασίαν τινὰ πρᾳότητα καὶ καταστολὴν τοῦ ἤθους καὶ φιλανθρωπίαν καὶ χρηστότητα καὶ ἡμερότητα ἐν τοῖς μὴ διὰ τὰ βιωτικὰ ἤ τινας χρείας ἀνθρωπικὰς ὑποκριναμένοις ἀλλὰ παραδεξαμένοις γνησίως τὸν περὶ θεοῦ καὶ Χριστοῦ καὶ τῆς ἐσομένης κρίσεως λόγον.
pass_a_gloss: After these things the Jew in Celsus says, as some learning-loving (φιλομαθής) Greek educated (πεπαιδευμένος) in the things of the Greeks, that 'the ancient myths (μῦθοι), having assigned (νείμαντες) divine sowing/descent (θείαν σποράν) to Perseus and Amphion and Aeacus and Minos (we did not believe even them, οὐδ᾽ αὐτοῖς ἐπιστεύσαμεν), nevertheless displayed (ἐπέδειξαν) great and wonderful works of theirs and truly beyond human (ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον), so that they might not seem unpersuasive (ἀπίθανοι); but you, what fine (καλόν) or wonderful (θαυμάσιον) thing have you done in deed or word? You displayed nothing to us, although we challenged (προκαλουμένων) you in the temple (ἱερῷ) to furnish some clear token (ἐναργὲς γνώρισμα) that you were the child of God (ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ παῖς)'. To this it must be said: let the Greeks show us of any of those listed (κατειλεγμένων) a life-benefiting (βιωφελές), brilliant (λαμπρόν) work, extending (παρατεῖναν) to later generations, and so great as to produce persuasiveness (πιθανότητα) for the myth about them saying they were born from divine seed. But they will show nothing, not even a little less (μικρῷ ἐλάττω), concerning the men whom he recorded, than the things which Jesus presented (παρέστησεν). Unless then the Greeks lead us back to myths and the histories among them, wishing us to believe those irrationally (ἀλόγως) but to disbelieve these even after much clear evidence (ἐνάργειαν). We then say that the whole inhabited world (οἰκουμένη) of humans holds the work of Jesus, in which sojourn (παροικοῦσιν) the churches of God through Jesus of those who have changed from countless (μυρίων ὅσων) evils. And further the name (ὄνομα) of Jesus removes (ἀφίστησι) derangements (ἐκστάσεις) of the minds (διανοίας) of humans, and demons (δαίμονας), and now also diseases (νόσους), and produces (ἐμποιεῖ) a certain wonderful meekness (πρᾳότητα) and composure (καταστολήν) of character and love of humankind (φιλανθρωπίαν) and kindness (χρηστότητα) and gentleness (ἡμερότητα) in those who have not pretended (ὑποκριναμένοις) on account of livelihood (τὰ βιωτικά) or some human needs, but have genuinely (γνησίως) accepted the word (λόγον) about God and Christ and the judgment to come (τῆς ἐσομένης κρίσεως).

lemmas.note: we did not believe even them

pass_b_english: After this, Celsus’s Jew, as though he were some Greek fond of learning and schooled in Greek literature, says: “The ancient myths that gave a divine descent to Perseus and Amphion and Aeacus and Minos (and even these we did not believe) still showed great and wonderful works of theirs, truly beyond human power, so that they would not seem unbelievable. But you, what fine or wonderful thing have you done, in deed or in word? You showed us nothing, although we challenged you in the temple to produce some clear sign that you were the Son of God.”

To this we must say: let the Greeks show us, from any of those listed, some work that was of use to human life, brilliant, reaching down to later generations, and so great that it lends credibility to the myth about them that says they were born of divine seed. But in the men he named they will show nothing that comes even close to what Jesus displayed; unless, that is, the Greeks lead us back to myths and to the stories told among them, wanting us to believe those without reason but to disbelieve these even after so much clear evidence.

We ourselves, then, say that the whole inhabited world of human beings holds the work of Jesus; in it dwell, as sojourners, the churches of God through Jesus, made up of those who have turned from countless evils. And still the name of Jesus drives madness from people’s minds, and demons, and diseases as well. And it produces a wonderful gentleness, composure of character, love for humankind, kindness and mildness in those who have not pretended for the sake of a livelihood or some human need, but have sincerely accepted the teaching about God and Christ and the judgment to come.

choices.choice: ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ παῖς ('the child of God') is rendered 'the Son of God', as the title the Jew is challenging. The Jew's challenge 'in the temple' to give a sign may allude to John 2:18 ('What sign do you show us?') or Matthew 21:23; uncertain, and the words are Celsus's, so not cited inline. 'Sojourn' (παροικοῦσιν) echoes common New Testament language for the Church as a sojourning community, without a single clear verse; uncited. 'The judgment to come' (τῆς ἐσομένης κρίσεως) is general Christian language (compare Acts 24:25), not cited. The parenthesis (οὐδ᾽ αὐτοῖς ἐπιστεύσαμεν) is Koetschau's punctuation, kept as an aside in the Jew's speech. ἤδη δὲ καὶ νόσους is rendered 'and diseases as well'. οὐδὲ μικρῷ ἐλάττω ('not even a little less than') is rendered 'nothing that comes even close to'.
'nothing ... that comes even a little short of' made 'nothing that comes even close to' (οὐδὲ μικρῷ ἐλάττω); the old wording could be read as the opposite
'drives distraction from people's minds' made 'drives madness from' (ἐκστάσεις διανοίας); 'distraction' was archaic in this sense
'put on a show for the sake of worldly gain' made 'pretended for the sake of a livelihood' (ὑποκριναμένοις; τὰ βιωτικά)
